interactions.summary: Jiang translates Dante's cruelty into a modern meritocracy story about a classmate hiding a Princeton acceptance letter, using it to argue that high-pressure winner-take-all cultures teach even friends to act like enemies.

speaker_notes.note: This student lands Jiang's intended abstraction by naming meritocracy as the social form that makes the betrayal intelligible.

claims.claim: Jiang's Princeton-envelope story is meant to explain Dante's cruelty by showing how meritocratic competition turns intimacy into rivalry.
A student says it is hardest to accept the elevation of someone closest to you because their success lands as a threat to your own equal standing.
Jiang says meritocracy is a winner-take-all, unforgiving culture in which only the best are appreciated and everyone else is effectively discarded.
Jiang uses Dante and Guido's poetic rivalry as another case of meritocratic pressure: the closer the rivals, the more likely one is to tear down the other's ascent.

signature_moments.moment: Meritocracy explains why the envelope gets torn up instead of celebrated.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: A student gives Jiang the exact modern social mechanism he wants for translating Dante's world into ours.

signature_moments.moment: A meritocracy is a high-pressure winner-take-all culture.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses Jiang's critique of modern social organization into a reusable diagnosis.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A winner-take-all system that intensifies envy and turns peers or friends into enemies by making status scarce and comparative.

chronology_notes.note: This packet is the lecture's first full bridge from Dante's Florentine world into a direct critique of contemporary meritocratic life.

uncertainty_notes.note: The anecdote contains minor ASR noise around school names and chronology, but the operative story is clear: a peer destroys a close friend's path upward out of status envy.
